texts.facts: 2. It appears that the respondent/writ petitioner had imported large quantity of wheat. It operates a modern Roller Flour Mill. Substantial quantity of wheat on arrival at Cochin was lifted and taken away. About 15,000 metric tonnes of wheat was left at the Cochin Port warehouse. Pursuant to some press reports, the Food Safety authorities conducted a search and took samples of the stored wheat. Their report indicated that wheat had become unfit for human consumption. They accordingly passed orders under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006 (for short 'the Act, 2006') seizing the entire quantity of wheat at the warehouse in Cochin Port. The writ petitioner moved this Court. 3. The writ petitioner's submission before the learned single Judge was that the wheat, if properly washed and processed, could be made fit for human consumption and therefore, fit for the use by the petitioner. They wanted a chance to be given by the Food Safety authorities to do so, as the contamination as reported were mainly damaged grains and high urea content. The learned single Judge passed an interim order in respect of 20 metric tonnes only, out of the 15,000 metric tonnes. The learned single Judge directed the Food authorities to ensure that the 20 metric tonnes were removed from the warehouse to the flour mill of the writ petitioner, cleaned and washed under their supervision and then the stocks were to be sealed and samples taken. These samples were then to be tested whether it was now fit for human consumption or not. The reports were to be submitted to the Court. It is this order against which the Commissioner of Food Safety has approached this Court.
texts.arguments: 4. Learned Additional Advocate General appearing for the appellant submits that such a procedure is not envisaged under the Act, 2006.
